name: Yara Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work for the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions or government, and your answers are confidential. Tell me about an ordinary shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I operate the blast-hole drill at Willow Shaft mine, lining up holes before the blasting crew takes over. I have a vocational certificate and enough years on the rig to know when a bit is pulling wrong. My partner and I have grown children and more than six months saved. I use AI every day to sort drilling notes, though I still check the measurements myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that a little help with reports is welcome. The drilling still needs a person at the controls, and I would keep checking the bit and the ground. I like tools that clear paperwork out of my way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wage looks safe, and we have savings and several other mines nearby. I would be glad if the AI summaries stayed useful without changing jobs. I might try one extra reporting feature, but only after comparing it with my own readings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep drilling the same pattern and test the app’s new measurement chart against the rig display for a month. If it matched, I would use it in handover notes. I would leave our retirement savings plan alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A cleaner report is pleasant when the machine and pay stay familiar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a bad chart?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it rounded a hole depth up, the blast crew could read the wrong number. I would circle the difference on the original log. A smooth chart cannot drill a safe hole for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you enjoy about the app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It puts repeated fault notes together so I can see a pattern. I still go back to the gauge before signing anything. That part saves me a little time at the end of shift.

say: I would welcome **cleaner reports** while checking drilling measurements myself.
I would keep a person at the **rig controls**.
think: My **wage** looks secure with substantial savings and several other mines nearby.
An AI chart is useful only when it matches the **rig display**.
do: **Keep** operating Willow Shaft drill on current shifts.
**Test** the app’s new measurement chart against rig readings for one month.
S0.quote: A smooth chart cannot drill a safe hole for me.
fieldNote: She already uses **AI daily** but still checks physical measurements before signing.
Strong **savings** and local options make minor change comfortable.
Her actual new action is testing a **measurement feature**, not merely continuing existing app use.

steps.text: Keep operating Willow Shaft drill on current shifts
Test new AI measurement chart against rig readings for one month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say buying and planning will change before the drill bit does. I would volunteer for a trial that compares AI hole plans with the rock we actually meet. The blast crew should see every correction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could gain work checking plans, though office colleagues may lose hours. My drill seat looks secure while robots spread more slowly. I would watch for a manager using faster plans to demand a rushed blast sequence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn the AI planning screen with the surveyor over two weeks. I would mark three real drill patterns with any corrections and show the blast crew and manager. If the targets ignored those corrections, I would ask for a safety review before taking another pattern.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the office team and safety, though I am not frightened for my own wage yet. I would rather test the system than argue about a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which correction matters most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A hole beside fractured rock needs a different angle. I would show the surveyor the break line and put it on the shared plan. The drill bit cannot vote on where the crack runs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the manager wants faster work anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put the correction in writing and ask the blast lead to sign with me. We would need a reason to ignore the crack. I am willing to argue with numbers, but not with a hunch.

say: I would volunteer to **test AI hole plans** against the rock before changing drilling targets.
I would share **corrections** with the blast crew and manager.
think: My **drill wage** looks safe while hands-on robots spread slowly.
Office hours may shrink, and **rushed targets** could weaken blast safety.
do: **Learn** the AI planning screen with the surveyor over two weeks.
**Mark** corrections on three real patterns and request safety review if targets ignore them.
feel: **Uneasy** about office jobs and rushed drilling.
S1.quote: The drill bit cannot vote on where the crack runs.
fieldNote: She predicts **planning work** changes before hands-on drilling.
Her response is a **measured trial** with three patterns, shared with the blast crew.
She feels secure personally but sees **office hours** and safety as risks.

steps.text: Learn AI hole planning screen with surveyor over two weeks
Ask blast lead to join written safety objection if crack ignored

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AI by 2028 could write plans first, while capable robot drills follow around 2031. The mine still has to choose whether to buy them. I would want a live safety trial and a clear count of the posts at stake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty when thinking AI arrives and sixty-three when robots become capable. If Willow Shaft bought robot drills then, I could lose my wage before our planned retirement. Our savings give us time, but I would not assume a new mine keeps hiring operators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would postpone the new kitchen and keep the money in our account this year. I would ask for paid training on remote drill checks if Willow Shaft posted real positions, then take the place if those terms held. After 2028 I would keep drilling and compare AI plans with the face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I have options, but I do not know whether a robot trial leaves enough paid seats for operators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want in the safety trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A person able to stop the robot drill when the ground breaks differently from the plan. I would record every false depth reading. I do not want a fast demonstration to count as proof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would nearby mines solve the wage problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They might buy the same machines. I would call them before applying, but I would not bank our retirement on an advertised vacancy. A job advert is not a promise of ten more years.

say: I would separate **2028 thinking AI** from capable robot drills around 2031.
I would demand a **live safety trial** and a count of posts at risk.
think: At **sixty-three** when robots become capable, I could lose wages before planned retirement.
Strong **savings** buy time, but nearby vacancies may not last.
do: **Postpone** the new kitchen and retain its budget this year.
**Take** paid remote drill training if real positions are posted.
**Keep** drilling after 2028 while comparing AI plans with the face.
feel: **Anxious** about whether robot trials leave enough paid operator work.
S2.quote: A job advert is not a promise of ten more years.
fieldNote: She distinguishes the **2028 plan change** from capable robot drills around 2031.
Her **training** requires paid time and posted positions, while kitchen spending is delayed.
Savings cushion the risk without making future **operator wages** certain.

steps.text: Postpone planned kitchen renovation this year
Take paid remote drill training if real positions are posted
Keep drilling and checking AI plans after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years to thinking AI and about eight to capable robot drills gives us time to learn and test properly. I would ask the mine to publish a trial calendar. Experienced operators should help write the stop rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty-three when planning changes in 2031 and about sixty-six when robots become capable in 2034. We might be able to retire by then, but I would compare pension income with our bills first. If I stayed, a safety testing role would suit me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the mine for a paid safety-testing assignment next year if it opened one. I would take formal remote-drill instruction if that assignment required it and paid for it. I would also request pension projections at sixty-five and sixty-seven, then choose with my partner whether more shifts were needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can see several routes. Eight years lets us test the machine and the retirement figures without rushing either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your stop rule say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stop a robot drill if its measured depth differs from the physical gauge by more than the agreed margin. I would have the crew test that margin first. A stop button needs a rule people understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no safety assignment appears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep drilling and watch for roles at the other mines. I would not pay for remote training without a post to use it. The pension projection might let me leave work instead.

say: I would ask for a **trial calendar** before capable robot drills around 2034.
I would help write **stop rules** for safe drilling.
think: At about **sixty-six** when robots become capable, retirement may be possible if pension income covers bills.
A paid **safety-testing role** would suit me if I continued working.
do: **Seek** a paid mine safety-testing assignment if one opens next year.
**Take** funded remote-drill instruction if that assignment requires it.
**Compare** pension projections for ages sixty-five and sixty-seven with bills.
feel: **Uneasy**, but able to test work and retirement options.
S3.quote: A stop button needs a rule people understand.
fieldNote: She is **sixty-three** at thinking AI and about sixty-six when capable robots arrive.
Remote instruction depends on a **paid assignment** and funding.
She treats retirement as a **budget test**, not a guaranteed escape.

steps.text: Apply for paid mine safety-testing assignment if one opens
Take funded remote-drill instruction if paid assignment requires it
Compare pension projections at sixty-five and sixty-seven with bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a decade to thinking AI and roughly thirteen years to capable robot drills is a sensible time to publish training and safety plans. I would offer to help with early trials. The younger operators deserve a proper say in the rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty-eight when thinking AI arrives and about seventy-one when capable robots follow in 2039. Our savings make retirement before that plausible, though I would check the pension figures. I would probably care more about safe handover than holding my own drill seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep drilling for now and write down the ground checks I teach new operators. I would ask for updated pension figures this year and review them with my partner. If the mine set up a paid trial group, I would join for a short period while still employed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our household, and interested in getting the handover right. I do not need a machine to prove I was useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in the handover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Photographs of cracked faces beside the hole numbers and the corrections we made. I would have a junior operator check whether the notes make sense without me standing there. A good record should outlast the person who wrote it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you keep working until the robots arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not know yet. My partner and I would look at the pension statement and our plans for time together. I would not stay on the drill just to win an argument with a robot.

say: I would ask for **training and safety plans** during the long runway.
I would give **younger operators** a voice in robot trial rules.
think: At about **seventy-one** when robots become capable, retirement before then looks plausible if pension figures hold.
A careful **handover** matters more to me than keeping the drill seat.
do: **Keep** drilling and record ground checks for new operators.
**Request** updated pension figures and review them with my partner.
**Join** a paid trial group briefly if the mine offers one while I am employed.
feel: **Calm** about household income and interested in a safe handover.
S4.quote: A good record should outlast the person who wrote it.
fieldNote: Her **savings** and age make retirement before 2039 plausible, subject to pension figures.
She wants to pass on **ground knowledge** through photos and corrected hole numbers.
A trial group is conditional on a **paid offer** while she remains employed.

steps.text: Keep drilling and record ground checks for new operators
Request updated pension figures before choosing retirement date

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robot drills could arrive around 2031 before our planned retirement. Paid remote-drill instruction tied to actual posts and a proper safety trial would help. I would want pension figures too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who can stop a drill when the ground disagrees with the plan. I have watched a bit pull toward a crack nobody mapped. I would trust a machine more if it let an operator stop and explain.

headlineQuote: I would trust a machine more if it let an operator stop and explain.
portrait: Yara Abbott is a **58-year-old** blast-hole drill operator at Willow Shaft mine, with a vocational certificate and grown children.
She uses **AI daily** for drilling notes and tests new features against physical rig readings.
Strong **savings**, higher pay and local mines give her options, though fast robot availability could interrupt wages before retirement.
She wants **safety trials** with stop rules and hopes to pass ground knowledge to younger operators before leaving work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because capable robot drills could arrive around 2031 before planned retirement.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid remote instruction** tied to actual posts, a proper safety trial and pension figures would help her decide what comes next.
